outcome: No event since 26 January 2024 that I could find changes what the conjecture asserts in general: it is still treated as open in general, with special cases proved between 1984 and 2011 and a 2012 structural result; the one 2026 AI-involved model-theory preprint I found (Freitag and Mutchnik, arXiv:2609.00436) concerns the stable forking conjecture, not this one.
problem_asks: The Wikipedia bullet gives only the name 'Kueker's conjecture' (citation [156], not reached), so this is written from the literature wording of the conjecture. Part 1: for every countable complete first-order theory T with infinite models, if every uncountable model of T is ℵ0-saturated, then T is categorical in some infinite cardinal (infinite power). Part 2 (Tanović's restated form, same claim): every Kueker theory, meaning a countable complete T with infinite models in which every uncountable model is ℵ0-saturated and T is not ℵ0-categorical, is ℵ1-categorical. The bullet asks the general claim over all such theories; special cases and classes are partial progress, not the bullet.

events.what_happened: Steven Buechler, 'Kueker's conjecture for superstable theories', Journal of Symbolic Logic 49(3):930-934, issue dated September 1984 (DOI 10.2307/2274146). Abstract (opened on Cambridge Core): 'We prove that if every uncountable model of a first-order theory T is ω-saturated and T is superstable then T is categorical in some infinite power.' No earlier preprint found; dated to the journal issue.
events.revisions: Cambridge Core lists 'published online 12 March 2014' for the 1984 article; the 1984 issue date is the earliest public date I could establish.
events.delivers: Confirms the conjecture's conclusion for superstable first-order theories: every uncountable model ω-saturated implies categoricity in some infinite power. Within superstable theories only.
events.remains: All stable-but-not-superstable theories and all unstable theories, i.e. everything outside the superstable class, in the general statement of the conjecture.

checked_by.who: Journal of Symbolic Logic (refereed journal of record)
checked_by.qualification: Refereed mathematical-logic journal; acceptance implies a referee's reading of the argument

events.direction: Proves the conjectured conclusion (categoricity in some infinite power) for the superstable class. Cuts in favour of the conjecture, within that class.

events.what_happened: Ehud Hrushovski, PhD thesis 'Contributions to Stable Model Theory' (1986), with a chapter on Kueker's conjecture. Per search-result summaries of the thesis text (the McMaster PDF returned binary to me, so I did not read it directly): the conjecture is proved for stable countable theories, where every uncountable model is ℵ0-saturated and T is ℵ0- or ℵ1-categorical; §2.3 proves it for theories interpreting an infinite linear ordering, described as 'our only excursion outside the domain of stability'; the thesis says the conjecture remains open for unstable theories.
events.revisions: Journal version 1989 (separate event, hrushovski-1989-jsl). The thesis is dated 1986 in search summaries; the 1989 journal publication is later and is not the first written argument.
events.delivers: Stable countable theories: every uncountable model ℵ0-saturated implies ℵ0- or ℵ1-categoricity (a sharper conclusion than 'some infinite power'). Countable theories interpreting an infinite linear ordering. Theories with Skolem functions are claimed in the 1989 abstract and in search summaries of the thesis; I did not verify the thesis for that case.
events.remains: Unstable countable theories that neither interpret an infinite linear ordering nor have Skolem functions. The thesis itself says the unstable case is open.

checked_by.who: Doctoral committee of the thesis (names not established)
checked_by.qualification: Thesis examiners for a doctoral degree
checked_by.what_they_did: Approved the thesis; inferred from its status as a PhD thesis, not verified

events.direction: Proves the conjectured conclusion for stable countable theories and for theories interpreting an infinite linear ordering. Cuts in favour of the conjecture within those classes; the author states the unstable remainder is open.

events.what_happened: Ehud Hrushovski, 'Kueker's conjecture for stable theories', Journal of Symbolic Logic 54(1):207-220, March 1989 (DOI 10.2307/2275025). Abstract (opened on Cambridge Core): 'Kueker's conjecture is proved for stable theories, for theories that interpret a linear ordering, and for theories with Skolem functions. The proof of the stable case involves certain results on coordinatization that are of independent interest.' This is the journal version of the argument in hrushovski-1986-thesis, so it is dated there under the date rule, not to 1989.
events.revisions: Journal publication March 1989; Cambridge Core lists 'published online 12 March 2014'. Dated to the 1986 thesis per the first-written-argument rule.
events.delivers: Same as hrushovski-1986-thesis: stable countable theories; theories interpreting a linear ordering; theories with Skolem functions (per the abstract, stated without restriction in the abstract as quoted).
events.remains: Unstable countable theories outside the linear-ordering and Skolem-function cases.

checked_by.who: Journal of Symbolic Logic (refereed journal of record)

events.time_since_posted: about 37 years for the journal version; about 40 years from the thesis
events.direction: Proves the conjectured conclusion for the stated classes. Cuts in favour of the conjecture within those classes.

events.what_happened: Vincent Guingona and Michael C. Laskowski, 'On VC-minimal theories and variants', arXiv:1110.4274 (submitted 19 October 2011; one version found). Section 3.1 (as rendered on ar5iv): weakly VC-minimal theories are stable or interpret an infinite linear order (Theorem 3.5). Corollary 3.6: a weakly VC-minimal theory in a countable language in which every uncountable model is ℵ0-saturated is categorical in some infinite power, the proof citing Hrushovski's stable and linear-order result. Introduction (ar5iv): 'we show that all weakly VC-minimal theories satisfy the Kueker Conjecture'. The arXiv abstract itself does not mention Kueker. The PDF was not extractable; the quotes come from the ar5iv rendering as summarised by my fetch tool.
events.revisions: One version (v1) per arXiv as fetched. Journal publication not established in my searches.
events.delivers: The conjecture's conclusion for countable weakly VC-minimal theories (a class of dependent theories lying strictly between VC-minimal and dependent), via the dichotomy stable-or-interprets-an-infinite-linear-order plus Hrushovski's theorem.
events.remains: Countable complete theories outside the weakly VC-minimal class and outside Hrushovski's cases, i.e. the general statement. The authors ask which other dependent theories share the stable / linear-order dichotomy and say they have no control over VC-density in weakly VC-minimal theories.
events.direction: Proves the conjectured conclusion for a class (countable weakly VC-minimal theories). Cuts in favour of the conjecture within that class.

events.what_happened: Saharon Shelah, 'Model theory without choice: Categoricity', arXiv:math/0504196 (v1 10 April 2005; v2 24 February 2007; v3 8 July 2008). Not a result on the conjecture: it uses Kueker's conjecture as an input. As rendered on arXiv HTML: 'So by Kueker conjecture (proved by Buechler ... for T superstable and by Hrushovski ... for stable T), we get contradiction' (§2), and 'as Kueker conjecture is known in the relevant case' (Introduction).
events.revisions: v2 24 Feb 2007; v3 8 Jul 2008 (per arXiv abstract page and HTML). Date given is v1.
events.delivers: Nothing new on Kueker's conjecture. Uses the superstable (Buechler) and stable (Hrushovski) cases as a black box in a choiceless proof that Łoś's conjecture is equivalent to Morley's theorem in ZF.
events.direction: Neither for nor against: it relies on the known superstable and stable cases and adds no new case.

events.what_happened: Predrag Tanović, 'On Kueker's conjecture', Journal of Symbolic Logic 77(4):1245-1256, December 2012 (DOI 10.2178/jsl.7704100; zbMATH Zbl 1266.03048). Abstract (opened on Cambridge Core and SANU record): 'We prove that a Kueker theory with infinite dcl does not have the strict order property' and 'strongly minimal types are dense: any non-algebraic formula is contained in a strongly minimal type.' Source of the restated form ('every Kueker theory is ℵ1-categorical') is Tanović's 2012 talk slides, which I could not extract. No preprint found.
events.revisions: Dates conflict across sources: SANU repository gives 1 Dec 2012 (issue); Cambridge Core gives 'published online 12 March 2014'; a search summary of Project Euclid gives first availability 15 October 2012 (Project Euclid page not opened). Recorded at year precision.
events.delivers: A structural restriction on Kueker theories with infinite dcl(∅): no strict order property, and strongly minimal types are dense. It yields no categoricity conclusion, so it settles no part of problem_asks.
events.remains: Whether every Kueker theory is ℵ1-categorical, including Kueker theories with finite dcl(∅) and those that do have the strict order property (the result rules out SOP only for infinite dcl(∅)).

checked_by.who: Journal of Symbolic Logic (refereed journal of record)

events.direction: Partial structural result on the hypothesis class of the conjecture; neither proves nor refutes the categoricity conclusion.

events.what_happened: Ziv Shami, 'On Kueker simple theories', Journal of Symbolic Logic 70(1):216-222, March 2005 (DOI 10.2178/jsl/1107298516). Neighbouring topic, not Kueker's conjecture: it studies a class named after Kueker, 'Kueker simple' theories (the paper's definition was not extracted by me). Results per the Cambridge abstract paraphrase: a Kueker simple theory eliminates ∃∞ and densely interprets weakly minimal formulas; generalises Hrushovski's dichotomy for almost complete formulas to simple theories; small unidimensional simple theories are supersimple of finite SU-rank.
events.revisions: Cambridge Core lists 'published online 12 March 2014'. Issue date March 2005 used.
events.delivers: Results on Kueker simple theories (a different class). Nothing on categoricity in an infinite power, so it does not bear on the conjecture.
events.remains: All of problem_asks. Recorded as a discard: same name, different question.

checked_by.who: Journal of Symbolic Logic (refereed journal of record)

events.direction: Not about the conjecture: a different class of theories that shares the name.

events.what_happened: James Freitag and Scott Mutchnik, 'A counterexample to the stable forking conjecture', arXiv:2609.00436 (submitted 31 August 2026; one version found). Neighbouring problem, not Kueker's conjecture. Abstract: 'Using ChatGPT 5.6, we find a counterexample to the stable forking conjecture. This answers a long-standing open question of Hart, Kim and Pillay (1996).' §1.1 (arXiv HTML): 'This is an AI-generated result proven with the help of GPT-5.6 Sol.' The counterexample T^¬StFk is shown to be simple, with forking unstable, so it is a counterexample to the stable forking conjecture. The full HTML text I read (about 200k of 206k characters) does not mention Kueker, Buechler or Hrushovski's Kueker results, and its only categoricity reference is to Morley's 1965 theorem in the introduction and bibliography.
events.revisions: One version found on arXiv (v1). Tracker record last checked 4 September 2026.
events.delivers: A negative answer to the stable forking conjecture (Hart–Kim–Pillay), by a two-sorted construction over modules for a quantum division algebra attached to a bipartite graph. Shares the stable-theory setting with Kueker's conjecture but no categoricity claim; does not bear on problem_asks as far as the text read shows.
events.doubts: Single preprint, not peer reviewed. A breakthrough tracker record says no independent specialist assessment, formal proof or separate construction was located as of 4 September 2026. The paper's AI-use statements are internally unclear (see ai). These are doubts about the stable forking result, not about Kueker's conjecture.
events.direction: Claims a counterexample to the stable forking conjecture. Not about Kueker's conjecture.
events.object: Per the abstract and §1.1: a counterexample to the stable forking conjecture, the theory T^¬StFk in a two-sorted language with a graph sort and a module sort over a quantum division algebra attached to a bipartite graph. Per the text, it is shown simple, with forking unstable (via an Erdős–Rado indiscernible-sequence argument), and is described as a direct axiom verification rather than a categoricity argument. The construction uses saturated models, so it is non-constructive in that sense. I read this through a fetch summary of the HTML, not the PDF.

systems.name: GPT-5.6 Sol
systems.what_it_did: The authors say the counterexample and its supporting proof route were produced by prompting the model: 'we prompted ChatGPT to construct a counterexample to the stable forking conjecture with a detailed series of prompts' (§1.1). A footnote says 'the arguments were based on proofs generated using JF's ChatGPT account'. The same §1.1 says 'proofs ... have been written entirely by the authors, and no AI tool was used in the actual writing of this manuscript', and 'AI was used for proofreading, with the edits performed and evaluated manually by the authors'. The abstract names the system as 'ChatGPT 5.6'. The paper's own statements do not fully agree on who produced the proofs.
systems.basis_quote: This is an AI-generated result proven with the help of GPT-5.6 Sol.

ai.disclosed_cost: Footnote: SM 'received a grant of access to ChatGPT Pro' through OpenAI's programme. No compute, token or money figures found.

summary: Nothing I found since 26 January 2024 changes what Kueker's conjecture asserts in general. The live Wikipedia list (model theory and formal languages section) still carries the bullet 'Kueker's conjecture' with citation [156], which I could not reach; there is no article at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kueker%27s_conjecture (HTTP 404). Because the bullet gives only the name, problem_asks is taken from the literature wording: for every countable complete first-order T with infinite models, if every uncountable model is ℵ0-saturated then T is categorical in some infinite power, restated by Tanović as 'every Kueker theory is ℵ1-categorical'. Partial results, each dated to its first written argument: superstable T (Buechler, JSL 1984, abstract opened); stable T, theories interpreting an infinite linear order, and theories with Skolem functions (Hrushovski, thesis 1986 and JSL 1989, abstract opened for 1989); countable weakly VC-minimal theories (Guingona and Laskowski, arXiv 1110.4274, 2011, Corollary 3.6 read through an ar5iv rendering, journal status not found). Tanović's JSL 2012 paper is a structural result for Kueker theories with infinite dcl(∅) (no strict order property; dense strongly minimal types) and gives no categoricity conclusion. Hrushovski's thesis and Tanović's slides are the sources for the statement that the general unstable case is open; I could not extract either PDF, so those statements rest on search summaries. Later work I could read does not settle the conjecture: the Pillay–Tanović 2025 survey on countable models (arXiv 2508.06854, HTML read, no mention of Kueker found, though the PDF was not extractable), Pillay's 2026 'Remarks on relative categoricity' (arXiv 2602.05866, full HTML read, no mention), and Goh–Tran 2026 (abstract only, no mention). Shelah's 2005 choiceless paper uses the superstable and stable cases as inputs and adds nothing. No AI system is credited with this conjecture in anything I found; Lean/AxiomProver/Aristotle searches, the Erdős-problem and AI-discoveries lists, and the news searches returned nothing on it. The one AI-involved model-theory preprint in 2026 that I found, Freitag and Mutchnik (arXiv 2609.00436, 31 August 2026), claims a counterexample to the stable forking conjecture, not to this conjecture; its text does not mention Kueker or categoricity in the parts I read (about 200k of 206k characters). Its AI statements conflict: §1.1 says 'This is an AI-generated result proven with the help of GPT-5.6 Sol' and a footnote says the arguments 'were based on proofs generated using JF's ChatGPT account', yet §1.1 also says the proofs 'have been written entirely by the authors'. I record it as a neighbouring discard. Close calls: (a) the 2011 weakly VC-minimal corollary is a case of the conjecture's own hypotheses, so I record it as a partial case rather than as noise; (b) Tanović 2012 might be read as moving a quantity the problem names, but its results are about the hypothesis class and it makes no categoricity claim, so I record it as structural only; (c) Freitag–Mutchnik is about a different conjecture (the abstract dates the Hart–Kim–Pillay question to 1996, while the paper's own bibliography entry is dated 2000), so I record it only for completeness. A 2024 SETTOP talk by Tanović, 'Countable models of a theory that interprets an infinite discrete linear order', is about counting countable models and not this conjecture, judging by its title and the search summary of arXiv 2212.13605 (2022, Vaught's conjecture); its slides were not extractable. Dates: the Buechler and Tanović journal dates conflict across Cambridge Core, the SANU repository and Project Euclid, so I used month or year precision as the sources allowed.
competing_reading: One could read the 2011 weakly VC-minimal corollary and Hrushovski's Skolem-function case as widening the set of countable theories known to satisfy the conjecture, and then read the 2012 Tanović result as moving the problem further. On that reading the problem is a partial-progress case, not an open one, and the general statement is open only in the unstable, non-linear-order, non-Skolem remainder. Against it, none of these later results gives a categoricity conclusion outside classes the conjecture already covered, and no source I read calls the general conjecture resolved. Another reading: the absence of 2024–2026 results is an artefact of a weak search index for arXiv math.LO, which I could not query directly.
what_would_settle_it: (1) Reading the full text of Hrushovski's 1986 thesis and Tanović's 2012 slides (both PDFs were binary to my tools) to confirm the unstable-case statement and the restated form. (2) Wikipedia's reference [156] for the bullet, which shows which source the list uses. (3) An arXiv search of math.LO for 'Kueker' filtered to 2024–2026, which I could not run; the search index did not surface any. (4) Full text of the Pillay–Tanović 2025 survey (arXiv 2508.06854) to check whether it cites Kueker's conjecture. (5) The zbMATH review of Tanović 2012 and Baldwin's Categoricity (2009) problem appendix, to check whether the conjecture is listed as open there. (6) Journal publication status of arXiv 1110.4274.

judgement.why: Every event that bears on Kueker's conjecture comes before the snapshot. Each one settles the conjecture for a class of theories (superstable; stable, interpreting a linear order, or with Skolem functions; weakly VC-minimal), so they are cases, not the whole statement. Hrushovski's thesis and his JSL paper are one argument, recorded twice: I scored both as cases. I left the thesis unreviewed because its committee is only inferred and is not named. Tanović 2012 restricts the structure of Kueker theories but proves no categoricity conclusion, so its scope is none. Shelah 2005 only uses known cases, so it is none too. Shami's 'Kueker simple' theories are a different question that shares the name, so that paper is a variant. Freitag–Mutchnik is about a different conjecture (stable forking), so it is a variant. Its AI role is marked generated from its own quote, but it does nothing for this problem.
judgement.doubts: The bullet gives only the name, so the statement is taken from the literature wording; Wikipedia's reference [156] was never reached. Hrushovski 1986 and 1989 are the same argument recorded as two events. The researcher could not query arXiv math.LO directly for 2024–2026 papers.
judgement.by: judging pass (JUDGE.md), claude-opus-5-5; not the researching agent and not a human reviewer
